ev1794092805596.title: Historical Documentation and Identification
ev1794092805596.description: The first documented references to the amphitheatre date back to the 16th century, when Ambrosio de Morales identified it in 1574. During this period, large stone blocks from the monument were reused in the construction of the Monastery of Uclés. In the late 18th century, scholars like Juan Antonio Fernández and José Cornide briefly documented its remains. By the 19th century, more detailed studies began to emerge, with definitive identification as an amphitheatre occurring in this period.

ev1794089962788.title: Integration within Segobriga Site
ev1794089962788.description: The amphitheatre is situated at the foot of a hill where Segobriga stands, approximately 60 meters west of the theatre, directly in front of the city's main entrance, known as the North Gate. Its transverse axis aligns with the cardo maximus and follows the presumed layout of the city. The building takes advantage of an ancient valley that drained water from within the settlement, influencing its quasi-circular shape.

ev1794086667118.title: Excavation and Stratigraphic Analysis
ev1794086667118.description: The excavation of the amphitheatre was initiated by G. de la Chica between 1953 and 1955. However, the most comprehensive excavation was conducted by Martin Almagro in the 1970s, particularly between 1973 and 1975. This work involved cleaning the entire monument and conducting several stratigraphic analyses for dating.

ev1794091097468.title: Design and Drainage
ev1794091097468.description: The amphitheatre is an example of a "filled structure" where the cavea is partially compartmentalised. The northern wall, being very thick, was reinforced with powerful pillars of large limestone blocks embedded in its opus incertum to resist the pressure of the earth. To mitigate the risk of excessive pressure on the upper part of the facade, this section was not filled with earth to its full height but instead used a structure of radial walls and filled vaults. The building drains through a sewer that runs along the axis of a vomitorium on the north side, adjacent to the minor axis.

ev1794088570468.title: Northern and Souther Cavea's Halfs
ev1794088570468.description:
The monument is constructed in two distinct halves with very different structures. The southern half of the cavea was built into the hillside. In contrast, the northern half of the cavea and both ends of its southern part were constructed on foundations of a more complex structure comprising three retaining walls that formed large "boxes"; the amphitheatre is situated at the foot of the hill. 
The arena and southern cavea are partially excavated into the ground. This method allowed the reuse of extracted rock to create blocks for the seating, which were supplemented with blocks from a quarry on the other side of the river Gigüela, near the Roman road in a lucus dedicated to Diana. 
The northern half of the building is supported by three thick concentric walls of opus incertum, forming a triple ring that follows the elliptical plan.

ev1794094714875.title: Seating Arrangement and Capacity
ev1794094714875.description: The amphitheatre of Segobriga is one of the smallest known, with an arena ratio of 1:1.22, a perimeter of 119.97 meters, and a surface area of 1122.45 square meters. The amphitheater's capacity was relatively small, with a cavea offering a proportionally reduced surface area. Using Golvin's index of 2.5 seats per square meter, the useful surface area of the cavea is approximately 2185.7 square meters, which would accommodate around 5460 people.

ev1794085697199.title: Access Points
ev1794085697199.description: The main entrances to the arena are through two large doors located at both ends of the longitudinal axis of the monument. Additionally, there is a small independent entrance on the eastern side that leads to a service corridor running along the northern side of the podium. This eastern entrance provides direct access to the arena from the theater and the main road leading into the city.

ev1794088259405.title: Arena Measures and Similar Structures
ev1794088259405.description: The arena measures 41.7 by 34 meters and has an irregular contour, being more rounded on the south side to save work in cutting the natural rock. This irregularity is also observed in other structures, such as Segobriga's theatre, as well as in the amphitheatres of Ampurias, Toulouse, and Ulpia Traiana. The arena lacks substructures and is accessed through two axial galleries: an eastern one wider than the western.

ev1794088402188.title: Construction Timeline
ev1794088402188.description: The amphitheatre of Segobriga was constructed during the reigns of Claudius and Vespasian. The construction techniques used for the amphitheatre are similar to those employed in the theatre, including opus quadratum for foundations and opus vittatum for walls with brick interlayers. This shared architectural approach suggests a coordinated planning effort during Segobriga's Augustan urbanisation.

ev1794088164327.title: The Amphitheater Inscription
ev1794088164327.description: An inscription found near the north wall of the amphitheatre, dated to 81 AD, suggests an initial phase of construction during this period. This inscription, though not found in situ, is likely associated with the monument. The amphitheatre was in use until the end of the third century, when a significant fire damaged its walls and stratigraphy.

ev1794087416381.title: Theatre and Anphitheater
ev1794087416381.description: The amphitheatre was constructed alongside the ancient Augustan wall, similar to the theatre. Both monuments are comparable in their construction era and structure, flanking the city's main entrance. However, unlike the theatre, there is no evidence of a longitudinal passageway covered by a vault between the amphitheatre and the wall.

ev1794091693268.title: Later Use and Destruction
ev1794091693268.description: During the Late Empire and Visigothic period, rudimentary dwellings were built within the arena, utilising stones from the seating area for their construction. This indicates intense occupation during this time. With the Arab invasion, further destruction and fires occurred in these simple structures, which contained reused Roman tiles and bricks.
ev1794091693268.eventMediaCaption: Muslim expansion in the Iberian Peninsula in the 8th century.

ev1794092641445.title: Monumental Architecture
ev1794092641445.description: The amphitheatre of Segobriga stands as a significant monument in the region, with an elliptical plan measuring 74 by 66.20 meters, covering an area of 3836 square meters. It features various architectural elements such as a podium, vomitoria, and carceres. The structure is notable for its complex construction and historical significance.
ev1794092641445.eventMediaCaption: View of the amphitheater of Segobriga

ev1794091587899.title: A Monument to Urban Transformation and Romanisation
ev1794091587899.description: The amphitheatre stands as a testament to Segobriga's significant urban renovation, transforming a modest Celtiberian oppidum into a provincial Roman city over just two or three generations. This rapid Romanisation was guided by a comprehensive urban planning strategy, reflecting an euergetic policy that led to intense construction activity. The amphitheatre is unique within the Tarraconense region, offering valuable architectural insights and documenting the city's extensive urban reforms.
